title: Lakeside CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Around Lakeside, most wells are about 29 ft deep with a 12 gpm median yield. Here’s what that means for drilling cost, water table, and buying land.
intro_html:
In the Lakeside and Mountain View area, most wells are shallow for the Front Range but still drilled into Denver Basin bedrock or nearby alluvial deposits. The state has records for 11,455 well permits within about five miles, and over half of those list a constructed well or a total depth.

If you’re buying a home on a well, or planning to build on a vacant lot around Edgewater, Wheat Ridge, or Berkley, it helps to know how deep wells usually go here, how much water they make, and what a new well is likely to cost before you commit to a property.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Lakeside
sections.html:
Within about five miles of Lakeside, the median total depth on record is only 29 feet, with the middle half running from 20 to 50 feet. That’s quite shallow compared to many mountain areas. About 87% of wells are under 100 feet, another 6% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 4% run 300 to 600 feet, and only 3% go past 600 feet. The deepest well on record makes it all the way down to 1,751 feet, so there are a few very deep completions in the Denver Basin sequence.

For a driller quoting your job, that 20–50 foot middle band is what they’ll expect for most domestic wells, but they’ll keep the rare deeper holes in mind when they price risk. Local geology is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock with some alluvial pockets.

sections.heading: Water table depth and long‑term trend
sections.html:
Static water level reports are fairly strong for this area, with 198 wells listing a depth to water. The median static level is about 13 feet below ground, and the middle half are between 10 and 20 feet. In practical terms, that means water is usually encountered not far below the surface, even when total well depth is deeper.

Looking at measurements over time, median static levels were about 15 feet in the 1950s, 18 feet in the 1960s, and about 13 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. That pattern does not show a steady decline; if anything, recent decades look a bit shallower than the earlier records. Around Twin Lakes and North Washington, you should still assume some seasonal fluctuation, but the regional data don’t point to a dropping water table.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water to expect
sections.html:
Yields around Lakeside are generally solid for household use. From 309 wells reporting a pump test, the median yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. That comfortably covers a typical exempt household well and modest irrigation if the permit allows it.

Only about 3% of tested wells come in under 1 gpm, and 8% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Most sit in the 5–15 gpm band at 54%, and 35% of wells test above 15 gpm. That yield distribution means low-producing or marginal wells do exist, but the odds are much better than in many hard-rock mountain areas. Still, I’d review nearby well logs carefully and have a new well tested before finalizing a purchase.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and permit activity
sections.html:
This area has a long history of well development. Permits per decade rose from 324 in the 1950s and 387 in the 1960s up through 490 in the 1970s and 523 in the 1980s. Activity then jumped, with 2,159 permits in the 1990s and 2,198 in the 2000s, followed by 1,704 in the 2010s and 859 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on record is from 2025, so drilling is very much ongoing.

Most wells are in unnamed fractured-bedrock or Denver Basin units, with some in Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium. About 55% of permits are for monitoring use, 26% for domestic or household, and 3% for irrigation. The most active drillers listed locally are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.), and Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.).

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost near Lakeside
sections.html:
In and around Lakeside, the subsurface is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, so pricing is fairly predictable. A typical drilling rate runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the median 29-foot depth, the drilled hole itself pencils out around $1,400–$2,000.

A complete new domestic well with casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and basic electrical usually lands in the $7,400–$14,000 range at that depth. Costs scale roughly with how deep the driller has to go, so those few wells that run hundreds of feet will be much more expensive. When budgeting for a vacant lot around Wheat Ridge or Edgewater, I’d use that finished-well range as a base and keep a healthy contingency in case your well needs to be deeper than the local median.

sections.heading: Key risks: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
Even with generally good yields, there is some risk. Around 3% of tested wells are under 1 gpm, and 8% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, which can feel tight without storage. Checking nearby well logs for depth and production is important, especially closer to older development.

On the water quality side, this corridor has a lot of industrial and legacy impacts. Within about ten miles there are 663 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 92 historic mine features, and 192 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Many of the 11,455 permits are actually monitoring wells (about 55%), which reflects that history. Before buying, I’d review any existing water tests, match your location against mapped environmental sites, and plan on comprehensive lab testing of a domestic well. Also consider septic setbacks and room for a replacement system when laying out a house and well on smaller parcels.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot around Lakeside
sections.html:
For a Lakeside, Mountain View, or Berkley property, I’d start with the Colorado DWR records: confirm there is a well permit, check the reported total depth, static water level, and yield. With a 29-foot median depth and 12.0 gpm median yield in the area, many homes are in good shape, but outliers do exist.

If you’re planning new construction, assume you’ll be in the common 20–50 foot depth band but be prepared financially for more. Verify what your well can legally be used for; around here, about 26% of permits are domestic/household and only 3% are irrigation, so lawn watering or livestock use may be limited. Given the number of monitoring and cleanup sites nearby, I’d make a full water-quality panel part of your due diligence, just like a home inspection.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Lakeside, Colorado?
faq.a: State records within about five miles of Lakeside show a median well depth of 29 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 50 feet. About 87% of wells are under 100 feet, 6% run 100–300 feet, 4% reach 300–600 feet, and only 3% go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record is 1,751 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Lakeside wells usually produce?
faq.a: From 309 wells with reported pump tests near Lakeside, the median yield is 12.0 gpm, and the middle half fall between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. Only about 3% of wells test under 1 gpm and 8% are between 1 and 5 gpm. Most wells, 54%, produce 5–15 gpm, and 35% exceed 15 gpm, which is generally strong for household use.

faq.q: Is the groundwater level dropping near Lakeside, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level data in the Lakeside area do not show a clear long-term decline. Median depth to water was about 15 feet in the 1950s and 18 feet in the 1960s, compared with about 13 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet again in the 2020s. The overall median static level from 198 measurements is around 13 feet below ground.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well near Lakeside?
faq.a: In the Lakeside area, drilling in Denver Basin bedrock typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 29 feet, the drilled hole is roughly $1,400–$2,000. A complete domestic well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical commonly ends up around $7,400–$14,000 at that depth, with deeper wells costing more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink near Lakeside, Colorado?
faq.a: Water quality varies by site. Around Lakeside there are many monitoring wells and mapped environmental concerns, including 663 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 192 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. That doesn’t mean every domestic well is contaminated, but it does mean you should plan on a thorough lab test of any existing or new well before relying on it for drinking water.
